segments.text: Welcome to your daily research news digest for November 23, 2026.
Today we cover AI team dynamics, LLM calibration, and effective machine learning rollouts.
Tune in for the details.
From arXiv - cs.AI, "Adding One More Agent: How AI Team Size and Formation Shape Productivity and Diversity in Human-AI Brainstorming Teams"

investigates how the number and formation of AI agents affect productivity and diversity in human-AI brainstorming teams, finding that the optimal number of AI partners depends on the desired outcome.
The study compared teams with one versus two AI partners against human-human dyads.
Experiments revealed that when humans paired with a single AI partner, the team generated more ideas, whereas the effect of the single AI partner diminished when two partners were introduced.
Furthermore, the presence of AI increased the global diversity of human-authored ideas, but a second AI was necessary to increase within-session differentiation.
Ultimately, the number and formation of AI partners significantly reshape human contributions to the brainstorming process.
This research indicates that the configuration of human-AI collaboration directly influences the quality and variety of creative output in team settings.
From arXiv - cs.AI, "Beyond Demographic Discrimination: Benchmarking Normative-Descriptive Calibration in LLMs"
details a study benchmarking Large Language Models on normative-descriptive calibration.
The research assesses whether models treat matched candidates differently when asked to describe an outcome versus decide one, revealing varying calibration behaviors across different models.
The study introduced the Normative-Descriptive Calibration Benchmark to measure this calibration across various Large Language Models.
Results indicated that some models, including Claude Sonnet and Opus, strongly separate these framings, while others, such as GPT-5.5, exhibited negative calibration.
This demonstrates that the separation of disparities and the prescription of those disparities are behaviors that vary depending on the specific language model architecture.
This research provides a framework for evaluating the internal consistency of LLM reasoning processes.
Further investigation into these calibration metrics is warranted for the development of more aligned artificial intelligence systems.
From arXiv - cs.LG, "Don't Discard Your Rollouts: Reusing Teacher RL Traces for Student Distillation"
details a method for reusing teacher Reinforcement Learning rollouts to distill knowledge to students, achieving performance comparable to canonical distillation without additional inference costs.
The research proposes treating rollout reuse as a data selection problem by utilizing metadata from GRPO to select student-compatible completions.
This involves ordering the data based on prompt pass rates and employing teacher log-likelihoods as a proxy for selection.
This two-stage recipe successfully achieves performance equivalent to canonical distillation across reasoning and coding tasks.
This development suggests a pathway to more computationally efficient methods for knowledge transfer in reinforcement learning models.
From arXiv - cs.LG, "LEAN: Library-Based Adaptation for Asynchronous, Federated Fine-Tuning"
reports a method for federated fine-tuning that utilizes a library-based adaptation technique to replace averaging.
The research demonstrates that this approach significantly outperforms averaging baselines when handling data heterogeneity and asynchrony in distributed settings.
Participants check out, locally fine-tune, and check back in low-rank adapters, which are then shuffled across sites for exposure to diverse data.
This method operates asynchronously and communicates only the low-rank parameters, thereby avoiding explicit aggregation of model weights across the network.
The process maintains a library of rank-one basis pairs rather than relying on averaging of fine-tuned weights.
This technique effectively manages the challenges inherent in asynchronous and heterogeneous federated learning environments.
The findings suggest a pathway for more robust and effective decentralized model training across diverse data sources.
From arXiv - stat.ML, "Communication-Efficient Federated Learning of Latent Patient Representations from Multi-Institutional EHRs"
details a method for learning shared latent representations from multi-institutional Electronic Health Record data through communication-efficient federated learning.

The approach utilizes a non-iterative federated spectral method where institutions share only aggregate marginal frequencies and a low-rank spectral summary instead of patient-level records to ensure privacy and minimize communication overhead.
A central server aggregates these summaries to reconstruct the shared low-rank structure and the direction necessary for recovering interpretable representations.
Simulations indicate that this methodology accurately estimates latent components and achieves superior performance compared to existing benchmarks when applied to stroke patient data.
This work suggests a pathway for discovering clinically meaningful, subgroup-specific patient representations across disparate healthcare facilities.
Future research will focus on the scalability of this approach in larger, more complex medical datasets.
From arXiv - cs.AI, "Towards Robust Partial-Edit Deepfake Localization: An edit and Generator Conditioned Analysis"
analyzes partial-edit deepfake localization using an edit- and generator-conditioned analysis of Segment-Aware Localization.
The research evaluated localization performance across different editing conditions categorized by content, meaning change, and editing operation.
The study found that localization performance is weaker on the SSR-Speech subset, and deletions represent the most challenging editing operation for both representations.
Single aggregate scores obscure these specific weaknesses, indicating that separate evaluation across generators and edit types is necessary for accurate assessment.
The work stresses the requirement for finer-grained analysis of partial-edit localization performance.
This research points toward the necessity for more detailed methods in assessing the robustness of deepfake localization techniques.
From arXiv - cs.AI, "AstronautBench: Measuring Agent Self-Improvement Across Episodes Through Knowledge, Evidence, and Progress"
details a benchmark for assessing agent self-improvement across episodes by measuring knowledge, evidence, and progress in an embodied world.

The benchmark utilizes the game Outer Wilds structure where knowledge persists across episode resets, focusing on what the agent knows, the evidence supporting that knowledge, and the agent's advancement.
Evaluations assessed reached locations, revealed facts, and the accuracy of answers to world knowledge questions.

Studies using different large language model judges indicated that these three metrics do not consistently align, demonstrating that correctness may increase without a corresponding alignment in the support from evidence, revealing limitations in simple progress tracking methodologies.
This work provides a framework for more nuanced evaluation of autonomous agent development in complex environments.
From arXiv - cs.LG, "Graph-XGB: A Hybrid GNN Framework for Outdoor-to-Indoor 5G Signal Reconstruction via Aerial-Only UAV RF Sensing"
details a novel framework for reconstructing indoor 5G signals using only aerial Radio Frequency sensing data, achieving the highest accuracy for RSSI and RSRP reconstruction.

The research introduces Graph-XGB, a hybrid Graph Neural Network framework that utilizes a modified SpiderGNN encoder incorporating a Floor-Aware 3D Distance metric to process UAV boundary measurements.
These measurements are mapped into a ten-dimensional manifold using Principal Component Analysis, which is subsequently fused with spatial features for prediction.
Independent, physics-tailored XGBoost regressors are employed to decode these embeddings, effectively separating the modeling of path-loss and interference dependencies.
Evaluation on real-world data demonstrated that Graph-XGB outperformed other architectures in reconstructing these 5G signal metrics.
This advancement suggests significant potential for deploying accurate indoor signal mapping using remote sensing techniques.
From arXiv - cs.LG, "Who Should Verify? Reviewer Selection with Partial Information and Outcome Audits"
investigates the cost associated with certifying procedures for selecting AI reviewers based on performance.
The research develops algorithms to identify the least costly certification method in hindsight when review data and answer keys have associated costs.
Experiments demonstrated that a targeted audit of review keys successfully reduced the number of keys required on specific datasets without compromising accuracy on others.
This work proposes methods for optimizing the selection and auditing of reviewers within machine learning environments.
The findings offer a framework for more efficient and verifiable systems in the development of artificial intelligence.
From arXiv - cs.AI, "Budget-Aware Predict-and-Verify Theorem Proving with Heterogeneous LLM Solvers"
details an agentic system for theorem proving that optimizes computation by managing heterogeneous large language model solvers.

Experiments demonstrate that this system, BudgetPV, allocates computation across subgoals and different LLM solvers using a cross-solver predictor, adjusting allocation based on feedback from verification steps to guide solver selection.
The methodology involves utilizing multiple theorem solvers with varying proving abilities and inference costs, and the system employs a predictor to manage the allocation.

Results indicate that BudgetPV requires less LLM generation computation than uniform allocation for equivalent tasks and achieves significant computation savings through the incorporation of less computationally expensive solvers.
This research suggests a pathway toward more efficient and cost-effective theorem proving in artificial intelligence systems.
And that's all for your research roundup of November 23rd, 2026.
Remember, more agents mean brighter ideas!
Thanks for diving into the deep end with us.
Until next time, keep questioning!
